passage: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through raindrops. The light bends and splits into many colors. A rainbow always shows its colors in the same order. You can only see one when the sun is behind you.

items.q: When can you see a rainbow?
choices: when the sun is behind you

passage: Camels are built for the desert. They can go many days without water. Their wide feet keep them from sinking in the sand. The humps on their backs store fat, not water, for energy.

passage: Ants are tiny but incredibly strong. A single ant can lift objects many times its own weight. They live in large colonies where every ant has a job. Together they build tunnels, gather food, and protect their queen.

passage: Some animals travel huge distances every year. This journey is called migration. Arctic terns, for example, fly from the top of the world to the bottom and back. They follow the seasons to find food and warmer weather.

passage: Most plants make their own food using sunlight, but a few are hunters. The Venus flytrap has leaves that snap shut when an insect lands on them. Tiny hairs sense the movement and trigger the trap. The plant slowly digests the bug to get nutrients the soil cannot provide.

items.q: How does the Venus flytrap catch insects?

choices: to get nutrients the soil lacks

items.q: How do most plants make their food?

passage: Earthquakes happen when giant pieces of the Earth's crust suddenly slip past each other. The ground shakes as energy spreads out in waves. Most earthquakes are too small to feel, but strong ones can topple buildings. Scientists use instruments called seismographs to measure them.

passage: Before electric lights, city streets were lit by gas lamps. Every evening, a lamplighter walked from post to post with a long pole, lighting each flame by hand. At dawn he returned to put them out. It was a slow job, but it kept the streets safe after dark.

passage: The rainforest is home to more kinds of plants and animals than anywhere else on land. Its tall trees form a thick roof called the canopy, where much of the wildlife lives. Very little sunlight reaches the shadowy forest floor. Sadly, large areas are cut down each year, putting many species at risk.

passage: Many birds build nests, but few are as clever as the weaver bird. Using its beak, it ties and knots blades of grass into a hanging home. The entrance faces downward to keep out snakes and other predators. A male often builds several nests to impress a mate.

passage: Thomas Edison is remembered for the light bulb, but his real genius was persistence. He failed thousands of times before finding a material that would glow without burning up. When asked about his failures, he said he had simply found many ways that did not work. His laboratory produced hundreds of other inventions as well.

items.q: How did Edison view his failures?
choices: as ways that did not work

passage: Long before satellites, mapmakers faced a difficult challenge: how to draw a round Earth on flat paper. Every method they tried stretched or shrank some part of the world. A map that showed the correct shapes distorted the sizes, and one that kept sizes accurate bent the shapes. Even today, no flat map is perfect.

Instead of relying on the sun, bacteria there make food from chemicals. Entire communities of worms, crabs, and clams depend on this hidden source of energy.

passage: For thousands of years, people measured time by the movement of the sun and stars. The invention of the mechanical clock changed daily life dramatically. Suddenly, towns could coordinate markets, prayers, and work by the ringing of a bell. Time became something shared and precise rather than a rough guess.

passage: Elephants communicate in ways humans cannot easily hear. Much of their sound is too low for our ears, rumbling through the ground over long distances. Other elephants feel these vibrations through their feet. In this way, herds separated by miles can warn one another of danger or find their way to water.

items.q: How do other elephants sense these messages?

passage: The printing of money rests on a fragile idea: trust. A banknote is only worth something because everyone agrees to accept it. If people suddenly doubted its value, the paper itself would be nearly worthless. Modern economies depend on this shared confidence far more than on the gold once kept in vaults.

items.q: Why is a banknote worth something?

passage: For centuries, doctors believed that illness was caused by bad air rather than invisible organisms. This idea led them to ignore the importance of cleanliness. Only after microscopes revealed a hidden world of microbes did medicine begin to change. Simple habits like washing hands went on to save countless lives.

passage: The tragedy of the commons describes what happens when many individuals share a limited resource. Each person, acting in self-interest, takes a little more, assuming it will make no difference. Collectively, however, their choices can exhaust the very thing they all depend on. Overfished oceans and polluted air are stark reminders of this dilemma.

items.q: What is the tragedy of the commons?
choices: shared resources get exhausted by self-interest
